 Buying forex for an international holiday: Should you exchange early or wait until departure?
 Airport forex purchases could cost thousands more, but buying foreign currency weeks in advance doesn't always guarantee savings either. 
 Priyadarshini Maji 
 November 18, 2026 / 18:32 IST 
 Story continues below Advertisement 
 Remove Ad 
 Last-minute forex at airports can cost Rs 5,000 extra.
 Compare rates 2 to 3 weeks before your trip.
 Check all fees, markup, and total payable amounts.

 Buying foreign currency at the last minute could make your international holiday more expensive than planned. In fact, a traveller purchasing $1,000 could end up paying over Rs 5,000 extra at an airport exchange counter compared with arranging forex in advance, according to an illustrative comparison shared by Niyo.
 But does that mean buying forex weeks before departure is always cheaper? Not necessarily. Exchange rates change daily, and purchasing early does not guarantee a better deal.
 Story continues below Advertisement 
 Remove Ad 
 Representative image: Forex Costs - Advance Purchase vs Airport Counter
 How early should you buy forex? 
 Vinay Bagri, Co-Founder and CEO of Niyo, says, "It is generally advisable to start comparing forex rates two to three weeks before travelling rather than waiting until the last minute."
 Story continues below Advertisement 
 Remove Ad 
 This gives travellers time to compare prices across banks, currency exchange providers and digital platforms rather than accepting whatever rate is available just before departure.

 However, buying early can work against travellers if the rupee strengthens later. The advantage of planning ahead is having more options, not necessarily securing the lowest exchange rate.
 How much can last-minute forex cost? 
 Story continues below Advertisement 
 Remove Ad 
 Consider a traveller purchasing $1,000 for an international holiday.
 In Niyo's illustrative example, buying dollars at Rs 95 each with a 1 percent markup would cost Rs 95,950.
 At an airport counter, assuming an exchange rate of Rs 97–98, a 4 percent markup and a Rs 500 service fee, the same $1,000 could cost Rs 1,01,380–1,02,420.
 That's approximately Rs 5,400–6,500 extra .
 Gagan Malhotra, Chief Operating Officer of BookMyForex, says airport counters typically offer less competitive rates, with travellers sometimes paying a premium of up to 10 percent for last-minute convenience.
 Actual charges vary across providers and currencies, so travellers should compare the final rupee amount payable rather than relying on advertised rates.
 Buy everything at once or in smaller amounts? 
 Splitting forex purchases over several weeks may help travellers avoid converting their entire budget at an unfavourable exchange rate. But it can also increase costs.
 "While staggered purchases can help average out exchange-rate fluctuations, they do not necessarily guarantee savings," says Malhotra.
 Multiple purchases may also attract repeated service or delivery charges.
 Bagri suggests converting the bulk of the requirement two to three weeks before departure while retaining some flexibility for additional purchases closer to the travel date.
 What other charges should you check? 
 Beyond exchange rates, travellers should compare transaction fees, delivery charges and applicable taxes.
 Those using forex cards should check issuance, reload, ATM withdrawal and cross-currency conversion charges. Currency bought for cash may also involve delivery and sell-back costs.
 The important thing is to compare the total rupees payable for the same amount of foreign currency, including all applicable charges.
 For most holidaymakers, planning ahead and comparing providers is more practical than trying to predict exactly when the exchange rate will be most favourable.
